diagnostic_evidence.quote: which we may compute in $O(k^2)$ time \cite{golubvanloan}
In particular, it requires $O(mk^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of times we form $B$.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper claims the k eigenvalues of B may be computed in O(k^2) time (citing Golub–Van Loan) and concludes the framework requires O(mk^2) computations/steps. Computing all eigenvalues of a k×k (symmetric) matrix costs Θ(k^3) with standard algorithms — the cited reference itself gives cubic complexity — and no O(k^2) algorithm exists. Each of the m trials needs O(k^2) kernel evaluations plus a Θ(k^3) eigendecomposition, so the total is Θ(mk^3), not O(mk^2).

failure_location.quote: This new framework requires $O(mk^2)$ computations, where $m$ is a constant that depends on the desired approximation accuracy.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the cost as Θ(mk^3) total (equivalently, O(mk^2) kernel evaluations plus Θ(mk^3) arithmetic), retaining the subquadratic-in-n claim for fixed k.
issues.overall_effect: The stated per-trial and total operation counts are understated by a factor of k. The headline subquadratic-in-n guarantee survives for fixed k ≪ n, but the specific complexity claims in the introduction, Section 2, and the conclusion are incorrect as stated.
issues.title: Complexity claims understate eigenvalue computation cost (O(k^2) vs Θ(k^3))
issues.why_classification: A local correction of a complexity statement; no theorem, method, rate, or the subquadratic-in-n scope is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Denote by $a_i$ and $b_j$ the $i$th and $j$th largest elements of $S$ and $T$, respectively
our assumptions are equivalent to requiring that $\mu_i=\nu_i$ for each $i=1,\ldots,k$, and therefore for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$.

issues.failure_explanation: Explicit counterexample: take k=3, n=6, T={1,2,30}, and let S be the three roots of t^3-2t^2+(5/4)t-7/30 (all in (0,1); ≈0.341, 0.770, 0.889) together with the three roots of t^3-64t^2+(4575/4)t-57364/15 (≈4.32, 27.75, 31.94). By Newton's identities Σ_{a∈S}a^r = 2Σ_{b∈T}b^r for r=1,2,3, so for A=diag(S), B=diag(T) we have tr(A^r)/6=tr(B^r)/3 for r≤k, with distinct nonnegative eigenvalues. Yet ⌈4k/n⌉=2, so the corollary requires σ_4(A)≥σ_3(B)=1, while σ_4(A)≈0.889<1: three of the six eigenvalues of A lie below the smallest eigenvalue of B, refuting the block-quantile claim under any ordering convention (the proposition as literally written is also inconsistent: it declares a_i, b_j the largest elements but uses b_0=0, b_{k+1}=∞ with ≤ inequalities — e.g. on the paper's own Figure 2 data, a_1=31 > b_2≈20.6 violates a_1≤b_2). The proof is independently invalid: it asserts that moment matching for r=1,…,k implies matching 'for each i∈ℕ', which is false (e.g. T={0,2} and S={0, 1.5, (2.5-√5.25)/2, (2.5+√5.25)/2} match the first two moments but not the third), and the determinant computations ('the b_i are precisely the roots of P_k', 'λ(x_i)=1/k') require moments up to order 2k-1, which the hypotheses do not provide.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair preserves the stated results; at minimum, a repair must strengthen the moment-matching hypothesis to order 2k-1 (making T the equal-weight Gaussian-type quadrature of S, for which a Christoffel-function/Chebyshev–Markov–Stieltjes argument can prove the interlacing) or drastically restrict the conclusion (e.g. k≤2), and must withdraw the advertised guarantee that the k matched moments suffice.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central structural result (the 'very general interlacing-type theorem') and Corollary 2.2 are false. The entire justification that matching k moments/traces yields eigenvalue quantile bounds (eq:interlacing) collapses, so the framework's core guarantee — meaningful bounds for all eigenvalues of A from the spectrum of B — is unproven and generally invalid, as are the abstract/introduction claims of proven efficacy, the 'very general interlacing result' claim, and the 'only subquadratic method' claim.
issues.title: Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.2 are false: k-moment matching does not imply the claimed interlacing
issues.why_classification: A central claimed theorem is false with an explicit counterexample; every supported resolution either abandons the stated theorem or excludes the regime (k-moment matching) on which the paper's framework and advertised guarantees are built, so major mathematical loss is unavoidable.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $\kappa$ must satisfy the condition of Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay} below for some $\epsilon>0$
Then, by our assumption on $\kappa$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay},
Hence, there exists a length scale $\lambda$ that makes $\kappa$ satisfy \eqref{eq:quickdecay}.

issues.failure_explanation: Eq. (5) is unsatisfiable as written: at s=1 (which lies in the required range [t,1], t<1) the displayed ratio equals 1, so 'ratio = s+ε' forces ε=0, contradicting the stated 'for some ε>0'; the proposition is therefore vacuous as stated. Moreover the proof needs a stronger, different hypothesis: its chain requires ∫_{[0,1/z_1]^l} ≥ ((1-ε)/z_1)∫_{[0,1]^l} (and the analogous upper bound), i.e. the two-sided RELATIVE bound ratio ∈ [s(1-ε), s(1+ε)]; an additive s±ε reading yields only 1/z_1 - ε, which is strictly smaller than (1-ε)/z_1 for z_1>1 (and the discrepancy is amplified by the large moments E(z^l)). Finally, the proof applies the condition at s=1/z_1 without ensuring 1/z_1∈[t,1]: the hypotheses on Ξ (eq:specialdistrib; Proposition 2.4 guarantees only nonnegative support) permit z=0 (where (1/z)^{1/d} is undefined), 0<z<1 (where s>1), or large z (e.g. 130.90, giving s≈0.0076), and nothing ties t to Ξ's support. The paper's satisfiability argument (a pointwise-in-s, additive Gaussian limit) does not establish the needed uniform relative bound at such small s.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate eq:quickdecay as the two-sided relative bound s(1-ε) ≤ ratio ≤ s(1+ε), valid for all relevant walks and all s∈(0,1] (or s∈[t,1] plus the added hypothesis supp(Ξ)⊆[1,1/t] with z>0 a.s.), and add the contained existence argument that such Ξ exist (e.g. a version of Proposition 2.4 with support in [1,∞) bounded by 1/t); the existing proof then yields eq:approxexpect.
issues.overall_effect: Proposition 2.3's guarantee (1-ε ≤ E(tr(B^r/k))/E(tr(A^r/n)) ≤ 1+ε), the only formal link between the sampling construction and moment matching, is unproven as stated; the framework's moment-matching step inherits the gap.
issues.title: Proposition 2.3's decay hypothesis (eq:quickdecay) is unsatisfiable as written and insufficient for its proof
issues.why_classification: A substantive restatement of the hypothesis plus new support/coupling conditions and a contained existence argument are needed — more than a local fix — but the proposition's method, conclusion form, and qualitative scope (rapidly decaying kernels) survive without new proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we scale each $y_i$ by a random number $z_i$
$Y$ is the set obtained by multiplying a random subsample of $X$ by a random scalar picked using $\Xi$.
we require each coordinate of $\mathbf{x}$ to be multiplied by $\delta=130.90$ with probability $d=1.4709\cdot10^{-6}$

issues.failure_explanation: Proposition 2.3 defines y_j ~ (1/z_j)^{1/d} U[0,1], i.e. each coordinate of a uniform point is multiplied by (1/z_j)^{1/d}, making y_j uniform on a cube of volume 1/z_j. The framework descriptions instead say to scale/multiply by z itself (the strategy list, Example 3's closing equivalence claim, Section 3's summary, and Section 4's discussion). Since the constructed Ξ is supported on values >1 (e.g. α≈4.87), multiplying by z yields points uniform on a cube of volume z^d rather than 1/z — a different distribution from the one analyzed, for which Proposition 2.3's moment calculation does not apply.

failure_location.quote: Note that this is equivalent to simply letting $Y$ be a random subset of points in $X$ scaled by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $\delta$ with probabilities $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$, respectively.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the prose in the strategy list, Example 3, Section 3, and Section 4 to state that each coordinate of a sampled uniform point is multiplied by (1/z)^{1/d} (equivalently, Y is uniform on a cube of volume 1/z).
issues.overall_effect: A reader implementing the framework from the strategy list, Example 3, or Sections 3–4 builds the wrong estimator (dilated rather than shrunk samples); the formal analysis covers only the (1/z)^{1/d} scaling.
issues.title: Construction misdescribed: points scaled by z instead of (1/z)^{1/d}
issues.why_classification: A local prose correction reconciling the descriptions with the analyzed construction; no formal result or guarantee changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: with respect to the Radon-Nikodym derivative $x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}$
Hence, the Gram matrix $H_{k,n}$ associated to $\{v_i\}_{i=0}^{(k-1)/2}$ in $V$ is positive definite.

issues.failure_explanation: With the stated weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}dx and v_i=√(n-k)(1-x)^{-(i+1/2)}, one computes ⟨v_i,v_j⟩=(n-k)B(n-k,k-l+1)=(n-k)!(k-l)!/(n-l)! for l=i+j, whereas the claimed identity requires (1/((k/n)C(n,k)))μ_l=(n-k)!(k-l-1)!/(n-l-1)!; these differ by the index-dependent factor (n-l)/(k-l) (e.g. n=7, k=3, l=0: 1/35 vs 1/15). Similarly, the w-chain with this weight computes (1/((k/n)C(n,k)))μ_{i+j} rather than μ_{i+j+1}. Hence the constructed Gram matrices are not the Hankel matrices H_{k,n} and H'_{k,n}, and their positive-definiteness — the crux of the proof — is not established by the displayed computation. The error is localized: with the weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^k dx (or, equivalently, shifting the exponents of v_i, w_i by -1/2), both displayed identities hold and the argument goes through.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}dx by x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^k dx (handling the trivial n=k case separately); both Gram identities then hold verbatim and the positive-definiteness argument completes the proof.
issues.overall_effect: The existence of the sampling distribution Ξ (for odd k with k|n) is left unproven by this argument, weakening the supply side of the framework; the statement itself remains true under the corrected computation.
issues.title: Proof of Proposition 2.4: Gram-matrix identities fail for the stated weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}
issues.why_classification: A single local correction (one exponent in the measure) repairs the computation with no loss of content, scope, or conclusion; the proposition and its role survive intact.
